title: Forgets to eat
hookLine: Confucius describes himself as someone so eager to learn he forgets his food (Analects 7.18)

lines: A MAN WHO FORGETS TO EAT.
cards: Somebody asks your friend what you're really like, and your friend says nothing. Just stands there. Later, you hear about it.
That's the scene in the Analects, the book of Confucius's sayings. A nobleman, the Duke of She, asks one of Confucius's students, Zilu, what kind of man his teacher is. Zilu doesn't answer.

When Confucius finds out, he doesn't scold. He tells Zilu what he could have said, and the portrait he offers of himself isn't of a sage or a statesman. Today's word is the student who stayed silent: Zilu.

teach.b: Why didn't you tell him, Confucius says, that I'm simply a man who, in his eagerness, forgets his food; who, in the joy of it, forgets his worries; and who doesn't notice old age coming on?
Three forgettings: food, sorrow, age. Second, what's being chased. The line itself just says eagerness, but Legge and the commentators read it as eagerness to learn.
Not power, not money: the steady work of study and practice that runs through the Analects. For Confucius, that work wasn't a chore to get through.
In this passage, it's what he loses himself in. Third, notice the joy. He doesn't forget food because he's grimly disciplined.
The joy of it makes him forget his troubles.
The eagerness comes first, and the forgetting follows. Nobody has to hide his tools or take away his plate. The hours just go.
Fourth, how this sits next to yesterday. Qing the woodworker had to fast for days to forget reward and praise. Confucius describes something that arrives on its own when the work itself is loved.

Two roads to the same quiet place, where the clock and the stomach go silent for a while. And the honest part: the Analects doesn't recommend skipping meals. Elsewhere it records Confucius as careful about his food.
This is a portrait of absorption, not a rule about lunch.
It can turn up anywhere: a puzzle, a garden, a song, and suddenly the window has gone dark.

how: Readers of the Analects, in Confucian schools and families and in classrooms, turn to this passage as Confucius's own picture of a life given to learning.

games.q: you're Zilu. a duke asks you what your teacher is really like. Confucius later tells you what you could have said. what was it?
o: he's the wisest man in the land.
he's a man so eager to learn he forgets to eat.
he's a great official who should be given office.
games.why: his self-portrait: a man who forgets his food in eagerness, forgets his worries in joy, and doesn't notice old age coming.

practice: Think back to a time you lost track of the hours doing something, recently or long ago, and let the memory fill in: what you were doing, where you sat, what your hands did.
Then ask whether something like it is within reach today, even for twenty minutes. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Zilu. The student who didn't answer when asked what kind of man Confucius was, and what Confucius told him he could have said. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: forget the hours. Joy first, and the forgetting follows. Day nine hundred two, done.
